questions.stemHtml: A 55-year-old woman with hypertension unresponsive to pharmacotherapy is diagnosed with stenosis of the right renal artery. During a procedure to place a stent in the renal artery, an intimal tear is accidentally produced that requires operative repair of the injured artery. Using an abdominal approach, it is necessary to elevate or mobilize which of the following structures to approach the right renal artery during this operation?

options.label: A
options.html: A. Duodenum, head of pancreas, celiac artery, right renal vein

options.label: B
options.html: B. Duodenum, head of pancreas, celiac artery, ureter

options.label: C
options.html: C. Duodenum, head of pancreas, splenic artery, right renal vein

options.label: D
options.html: D. Right colic flexure, duodenum, head of pancreas, right renal vein

options.label: E
options.html: E. Right colic flexure, duodenum, head of pancreas, ureter

options.label: F
options.html: F. Right colic flexure, head of pancreas, splenic artery, ureter

questions.explanationHtml:
Correct Answer: D.

Educational Objective: The renal artery originates from the aorta inferior to the superior mesenteric artery around the level of L1-L2. Using an abdominal approach to access the right renal artery, the right colic flexure, duodenum, head of pancreas, and right renal vein would need to be mobilized or elevated.

Key Concept: The renal artery originates from the aorta and is the primary blood supply to the kidney.

Explanation: The aorta and renal artery are retroperitoneal structures that lie deep to the abdominal contents. The renal artery often branches from the aorta at the level of L1-L2 and courses posteriorly to the renal vein. To obtain adequate exposure to the renal artery when using an abdominal approach, the right colic flexure, duodenum, head of pancreas, right renal vein, and possibly the liver may require elevation or mobilization.

Differential: This patient is undergoing repair of the right renal artery using an abdominal approach. The right colic flexure, duodenum, head of pancreas, and right renal vein are often needed to be elevated or mobilized to access the structure. The celiac artery, the ureter, and the splenic artery would not likely need to be elevated or mobilized during this procedure, making the other options incorrect.

Incorrect Answers: A, B, C, E, and F.

Choice A: Duodenum, head of pancreas, celiac artery, right renal vein is incorrect. The celiac artery arises superiorly from the renal arteries. The celiac artery would not likely need to be elevated or mobilized.

Choice B: Duodenum, head of pancreas, celiac artery, ureter is incorrect. The ureter arises from the kidney posterior to the renal artery and vein. The ureter would not likely need to be mobilized or elevated during this procedure.

Choice C: Duodenum, head of pancreas, splenic artery, right renal vein is incorrect. The splenic artery is a branch of the celiac artery that arises superiorly from the renal arteries. The splenic artery would not likely need to be mobilized or elevated during the surgery.

Choice E: Right colic flexure, duodenum, head of pancreas, ureter is incorrect. The ureter arises from the kidney posterior to the renal artery and vein. The ureter would not need to be mobilized or elevated during this procedure.

Choice F: Right colic flexure, head of pancreas, splenic artery, ureter is incorrect. The splenic artery is a branch of the celiac artery that arises superiorly from the renal arteries. The splenic artery would not likely need to be mobilized or elevated during the surgery.

questions.stemHtml: A 22-year-old man who is a boxer comes to the physician for removal of an intraoral wire fixation. Eight weeks ago, he sustained bilateral fractures of the neck of the mandibular condyle from a punch to his chin. After the physician removes the wires, the patient is unable to voluntarily open his jaw. When the jaw is manually opened, he is able to close it with appropriate force. X-rays show adequate bone healing and alignment. Which of the following muscles was most likely damaged during the original injury to this patient?
questions.explanationHtml:
Correct Answer: B.

Educational Objective: The lateral pterygoid is the primary muscle that opens the jaw. The lateral pterygoid inserts on the neck of the mandibular condyle, and a fracture to this area can impair jaw opening.

Key Concept: Jaw opening can be impaired due to a fracture of the neck of the mandibular condyle, where the lateral pterygoid inserts.

Explanation: The lateral pterygoid is the major muscle (and only muscle of mastication) that opens the jaw. The lateral pterygoid originates along the inferior sphenoid and attaches along the neck of the mandibular condyle. Fracture of the mandibular condyle can result in damage to the lateral pterygoid at the insertion site.

Differential: The patient presents with impaired jaw opening after a neck of the mandibular condyle fracture. The lateral pterygoid is the muscle that attaches at the neck of the mandibular condyle and opens the jaw. The other muscles of mastication, including the masseter, temporalis, and medial pterygoid, all close the jaw.

Incorrect Answers: A, C, D, E, and F.

Choice A: Buccinator is incorrect. The buccinator tenses the cheeks during mastication and does not open the jaw. Buccinator injury would be unlikely to arise from mandibular condyle fracture.

Choices C, D, and F: Masseter, medial pterygoid, and temporalis are incorrect. The masseter, medial pterygoid, and temporalis are muscles of mastication that function to close the jaw. Jaw closure is intact in this patient’s case.

Choice E: Mylohyoid is incorrect. The mylohyoid forms the muscular floor of the oral cavity and does not attach at the neck of the mandibular condyle. While the mylohyoid can depress the jaw slightly by elevating the hyoid, this is a minor contributor to jaw opening.

questions.stemHtml: A 19-year-old woman, gravida 1, para 1, develops a fever, chills, and moderate lower abdominal pain in the hospital 3 days after cesarean delivery of a healthy female newborn at term. She has not had any urinary symptoms. Pregnancy was complicated by chlamydia, which was treated at her first prenatal visit, and recurrent urinary tract infections. Current medication is only a prenatal vitamin. She had smoked one pack of cigarettes daily for 2 years but quit 9 months ago when she found out she was pregnant. Temperature is 38.5°C (101.3°F), pulse is 109/min, respirations are 16/min, and blood pressure is 108/72 mm Hg. Pulse oximetry on room air shows an oxygen saturation of 97%. The fundus is tender to palpation, but there is no erythema or drainage of the incision. Lochia is malodorous and yellow-green. The remainder of the physical examination shows no abnormalities. Which of the following historical factors has most likely increased this patient's risk for developing her current condition?
questions.explanationHtml:
Correct Answer: B.

Educational Objective: Cesarean delivery most likely increased this patient's risk for developing postpartum endometritis due to the risk it presents for bacterial inoculation of the uterine cavity.

Evaluation: This patient develops fever, tachycardia, uterine fundal tenderness, and malodorous lochia 3 days after cesarean delivery, which is consistent with postpartum endometritis.

Definition: Postpartum endometritis is a polymicrobial infection of the decidua that occurs after delivery, especially following cesarean or instrumented delivery. Surgical disruption of the uterine barrier allows ascending vaginal flora to infect the endometrium. Common organisms include anaerobes, gram-negative rods, and Streptococcus species. Endometritis typically presents within 2 to 3 days postpartum.

Prevention: Prophylactic antibiotics given before cesarean delivery decrease the risk for postpartum endometritis. Maintaining sterile technique during delivery helps prevent infection.

Treatment: Treatment consists of intravenous broad-spectrum antibiotics, typically clindamycin and gentamicin, until the patient is afebrile for at least 24 hours, at which point oral antibiotics are initiated.

Differential: Cesarean delivery dramatically increases the risk for postpartum endometritis compared to vaginal delivery, making it the most significant historical risk factor for this patient.

Incorrect Answers: A, C, D, and E.

Choice A: Age is not the most significant historical risk factor. Young maternal age is not a known independent risk factor for postpartum endometritis.

Choice C: Previous episode of chlamydia is incorrect. Prior treated chlamydia does not significantly increase the risk for postpartum endometritis. Once the infection has been treated, the causative bacteria is no longer present to contribute to subsequent infection.

Choice D: Recurrent urinary tract infections is not the most significant historical risk factor. Urinary tract infections are unrelated to uterine infection in the postpartum period. Unless the patient is immunocompromised, which this patient is not, there is no direct connection between a urinary tract infection and endometritis.

Choice E: Tobacco use is incorrect. Smoking is associated with poor wound healing and is a risk factor for placental abruption and low birth weight; however, it is not a major risk factor for postpartum endometritis.

questions.stemHtml: A 61-year-old woman is given capsaicin for treatment of postherpetic neuralgia. This treatment depletes which of the following peptides from sensory nerve endings?
questions.explanationHtml:
Correct Answer: D.

Educational Objective: Capsaicin relieves neuropathic pain by desensitizing nociceptive sensory neurons through depletion of substance P from peripheral nerve endings.

Evaluation: This patient is being treated for postherpetic neuralgia, a chronic neuropathic pain condition that arises from nerve injury after herpes zoster infection. Capsaicin is used not to reverse the underlying disease process, but to decrease pain transmission at the level of primary sensory afferents.

Definition: Capsaicin activates the transient receptor potential vanilloid 1 (TRPV1) channel on unmyelinated C fibers and some A delta fibers. Initial activation causes depolarization and burning pain, but repeated or sustained exposure leads to functional desensitization of these neurons. This occurs through depletion of substance P, a key neuropeptide involved in nociceptive signal transmission and neurogenic inflammation. Loss of substance P decreases pain signaling from peripheral tissues to the central nervous system, producing analgesia.

Prevention: There is no prevention for postherpetic neuralgia itself, but early antiviral treatment of herpes zoster decreases risk.

Treatment: Capsaicin is used as a topical or localized therapy to decrease neuropathic pain by exhausting substance P stores and diminishing nociceptor responsiveness.

Differential: Other neuropathic pain treatments act centrally or on ion channels, whereas capsaicin uniquely works by peripheral neuropeptide depletion at sensory nerve endings.

Incorrect Answers: A, B, C, and E.

Choice A: Bradykinin is incorrect. Bradykinin is an inflammatory mediator that sensitizes pain receptors but is not stored or depleted from sensory nerve endings by capsaicin.

Choice B: Calcitonin gene-related peptide is incorrect. Calcitonin gene-related peptide is involved in vasodilation and migraine pathophysiology and is not the primary neuropeptide depleted by capsaicin.

Choice C: Neuropeptide Y is incorrect. Neuropeptide Y is involved in autonomic regulation and appetite control rather than peripheral nociceptive pain transmission.

Choice E: Vasoactive intestinal peptide is incorrect. Vasoactive intestinal peptide is associated with smooth muscle relaxation and parasympathetic signaling, not nociceptive sensory neuron depletion.

questions.stemHtml: A 20-year-old man has headaches and vomiting. Findings on physical examination are unremarkable except for a bitemporal hemianopia. Serum concentrations of prolactin, growth hormone, and follicle-stimulating hormone are within the reference ranges. CT scans of the head show a 3-cm focally calcified cystic suprasellar mass. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanationHtml:
Correct Answer: C.

Educational Objective: The most likely diagnosis for this patient with a calcified cystic suprasellar mass, bitemporal hemianopia, and normal pituitary hormone concentrations is craniopharyngioma.

Evaluation: This patient presents with headaches, vomiting, and bitemporal hemianopia, indicating increased intracranial pressure and optic chiasm compression. CT scans of the head show a focally calcified, cystic mass in the suprasellar region, a classic radiographic pattern for craniopharyngioma. Normal pituitary hormone concentrations argue against a functioning pituitary tumor and support a mass effect rather than hormone hypersecretion.

Definition: Craniopharyngioma is a benign but locally aggressive epithelial tumor derived from remnants of Rathke pouch. It commonly arises in the suprasellar region and often contains cystic components and calcifications. Growth leads to compression of the optic chiasm, causing visual field defects, and may eventually disrupt hypothalamic or pituitary function. Despite benign histology, recurrence and morbidity are common due to proximity to critical structures.

Prevention: There are no established preventive measures, as craniopharyngioma arises from developmental remnants.

Treatment: Management typically involves surgical resection with or without adjunctive radiation therapy, balancing tumor control with preservation of neurologic and endocrine function.

Differential: Suprasellar tumors are distinguished by location, calcification, cystic architecture, and endocrine activity, with craniopharyngioma characteristically showing calcifications and mass effect without hormone hypersecretion.

Incorrect Answers: A, B, D, and E.

Choice A: Chordoma is incorrect. Chordomas arise from notochord remnants at the clivus or sacrum and cause local bone destruction rather than suprasellar cystic masses with calcifications.

Choice B: Choroid plexus papilloma is incorrect. These tumors arise within the ventricular system and present with hydrocephalus due to cerebrospinal fluid overproduction, not optic chiasm compression.

Choice D: Ependymoma is incorrect. Ependymomas originate from ventricular lining cells and are typically located in the fourth ventricle in children or the spinal cord in adults, not the suprasellar region.

Choice E: Pituitary adenoma is incorrect. Pituitary adenomas usually present with hormone hypersecretion or hypopituitarism and are solid, noncalcified lesions arising within the sella turcica rather than cystic suprasellar masses.

questions.stemHtml: A 3-year-old boy is brought to the physician because of a 5-day history of yellow-tinged skin. Physical examination shows jaundice and hepatomegaly. Serum liver enzyme activities are mildly increased. Serologic testing for viral hepatitis is negative. Further testing shows a decreased plasma α1-antitrypsin concentration, and an isoelectric focusing study result shows the protease inhibitor ZZ genotype. Which of the following processes is most likely occurring in this patient's hepatocytes?

options.label: A
options.html: A. Crystallization of the mutant protein, resulting in cytotoxicity

options.label: B
options.html: B. Expression of the mutant protein on the cell surface, leading to immune-mediated cytotoxicity

options.label: C
options.html: C. Increased elastase activity, resulting in autolysis of hepatocytes

options.label: D
options.html: D. Malignant transformation and hyperproliferation, resulting in neoplasia

options.label: E
options.html: E. Misfolding of the mutant protein, leading to endoplasmic reticulum stress and apoptosis

questions.explanationHtml:
Correct Answer: E.

Educational Objective: In this young child who presents with jaundice, hepatosplenomegaly, transaminitis, and decreased plasma α1-antitrypsin concentration, the most likely abnormal process in his hepatocytes is the misfolding of the mutant protein, leading to endoplasmic reticulum stress and apoptosis. This patient has α1-antitrypsin deficiency, a common cause of early-onset obstructive lung disease and cirrhosis.

Evaluation: Children who develop hepatosplenomegaly, jaundice, and increased liver enzymes should be evaluated for α1-antitrypsin deficiency among other causes (eg, malignancy, hepatitis). In severe cases of α1-antitrypsin deficiency, patients may develop liver failure and obstructive pulmonary disease.

Definition: α1-Antitrypsin deficiency is an autosomal codominant disease. Patients may inherit one or two abnormal alleles, which affects the timing of clinical presentation and disease severity. α1-Antitrypsin is a protease inhibitor produced by the liver and protects the liver and lungs from damage caused by neutrophilic elastase. In patients with a mutant allele, there is protein misfolding, leading to intracellular accumulation and cell death. Patients with two abnormal alleles present with a severe phenotype.

Prevention: In patients with α1-antitrypsin deficiency, abstinence from smoking is recommended to prevent worsening of the condition.

Treatment: In patients with severe liver disease, transplantation is recommended. In patients with lung involvement, oral glucocorticoids and bronchodilators may be recommended. In patients with severe lung involvement, infusion of pooled plasma-purified human α1-antitrypsin may be beneficial. Patients with severe pulmonary disease may also require transplantation.

Differential: In this child with hepatosplenomegaly and abnormal α1-antitrypsin concentration, the most likely cause is α1-antitrypsin deficiency. Abnormal alleles cause the misfolding of α1-antitrypsin, accumulation in hepatocytes, and eventual apoptosis.

Incorrect Answers: A, B, C, and D.

Choice A: Crystallization of the mutant protein, resulting in cytotoxicity is incorrect. Crystallization of proteins may occur in lysosomal storage diseases. This patient’s presentation is caused by α1-antitrypsin deficiency associated with the misfolding and accumulation of the protein within the cell, triggering apoptosis.

Choice B: Expression of the mutant protein on the cell surface, leading to immune-mediated cytotoxicity is incorrect. This mechanism has been associated with the development of eosinophilic disease. The patient’s presentation is consistent with α1-antitrypsin deficiency.

Choice C: Increased elastase activity, resulting in autolysis of hepatocytes is incorrect. Increased elastase activity is associated with smoking. In patients with α1-antitrypsin disease, the issue is decreased antitrypsin protein concentrations or function, not increased elastase activity. In all patients, especially those with α1-antitrypsin deficiency, abstinence from smoking is recommended.

Choice D: Malignant transformation and hyperproliferation, resulting in neoplasia is incorrect. This is a common pathway in the origin of various forms of cancer. The patient’s findings are consistent with α1-antitrypsin disease as opposed to newly diagnosed cancer.

questions.stemHtml: A 38-year-old man comes to the physician because of a 6-month history of shortness of breath with exertion and nonproductive cough. He has smoked one-half pack of cigarettes daily for 20 years. There is a family history of respiratory disease. He is 178 cm (5 ft 10 in) tall and weighs 59 kg (130 lb); BMI is 19 kg/m2. His pulse is 80/min, respirations are 18/min, and blood pressure is 105/90 mm Hg. Physical examination shows no cyanosis. A chest x-ray shows hyperinflated lungs with a flattened diaphragm. Serum studies show a markedly decreased α1-antitrypsin activity. As this patient's disease progresses, which of the following pulmonary findings will most likely decrease?

options.label: B
options.html: B. Diffusing capacity for carbon monoxide

questions.explanationHtml:
Correct Answer: B.

Educational Objective: α1-Antitrypsin deficiency causes early-onset emphysema due to unchecked neutrophil elastase activity, leading to destruction of alveolar walls. As this patient's disease progresses, the diffusing capacity of the lungs for carbon monoxide (DLCO) decreases due to loss of alveolar-capillary surface area.

Key Concept: Emphysema is a chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) characterized by destruction of alveolar walls, resulting in decreased alveolar-capillary surface area for gas exchange. DLCO is directly proportional to the available alveolar-capillary membrane area, thus, DLCO decreases as COPD worsens.

Explanation: This 38-year-old patient has early-onset panacinar emphysema caused by α1-antitrypsin deficiency, which is strongly associated with liver disease. questions.stemHtml: A 15-year-old boy is brought to the emergency department because of a 1-day history of fever and a cough productive of blood-tinged sputum. He has no history of serious illness and takes no medications. He appears feverish. Temperature is 40.0°C (104.0°F), pulse is 112/min, respirations are 25/min, and blood pressure is 110/70 mm Hg. Pulse oximetry on room air shows an oxygen saturation of 88%. Physical examination shows dullness over the left lower lung field. Leukocyte count is 17,000/mm3. Chest x-ray shows an infiltrate in the left lower lobe with air bronchograms. Which of the following enzymes plays a critical role in the bactericidal apparatus in the inflammatory cells involved in this patient's condition?
questions.explanationHtml:
Correct Answer: D.

Educational Objective: Bacterial pneumonia triggers a neutrophil-mediated inflammatory response, with neutrophils killing ingested pathogens through reactive oxygen species. Myeloperoxidase (MPO) is a key enzyme in neutrophils that produce hypochlorous acid (bleach) from hydrogen peroxide, enabling bacterial killing.

Key Concept: The bactericidal activity of neutrophils relies on the respiratory burst, during which nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide phosphate oxidase generates superoxide, which is converted to hydrogen peroxide. MPO then uses hydrogen peroxide to create hypochlorous acid, a powerful antimicrobial agent used to destroy bacteria inside phagolysosomes.

Explanation: This patient presents with pneumonia, evidenced by fever, productive cough, hypoxia, leukocytosis, and a lobar infiltrate with air bronchograms, indicating alveolar filling with inflammatory exudate. Neutrophils are the primary inflammatory cells in bacterial pneumonia. They migrate to infected alveoli and phagocytose bacteria. The respiratory burst in neutrophils produces reactive oxygen species, and MPO is essential for converting hydrogen peroxide into hypochlorous acid, which is microbicidal.

Differential: The patient’s presentation is most suggestive of bacterial pneumonia, which is driven by neutrophil oxidative killing. Therefore, MPO is the most likely enzyme playing a critical role in the bactericidal apparatus in the inflammatory cells in this setting.

Incorrect Answers: A, B, C, and E.

Choice A: Catalase is incorrect. Catalase is an enzyme produced by some bacteria to neutralize hydrogen peroxide and is a virulence factor/method of evading the host immune defense. Catalase is not a component of the neutrophil respiratory (oxidative) burst.

Choice B: Ceruloplasmin is incorrect. Ceruloplasmin is a plasma protein that binds copper. It is not directly involved in the neutrophil respiratory burst.

Choice C: Interferon gamma is incorrect. Interferon gamma is a macrophage-activating cytokine and is important in the management of intracellular infections such as tuberculosis and hepatitis. It does not play a role in the neutrophil respiratory burst.

Choice E: Superoxide dismutase is incorrect. Superoxide dismutase converts superoxide into hydrogen peroxide inside cells, but it is not the key bactericidal enzyme in the inflammatory cells involved in this patient's condition. MPO plays a critical role in the conversion of hydrogen peroxide into hypochlorous acid.

After greeting the patient, which of the following is the most appropriate initial statement by the physician?

questions.explanationHtml:
Correct Answer: E.

Educational Objective: When facing time limitations, physicians should collaborate with patients to set priorities for the visit. The most appropriate initial statement by the physician to this patient with many presenting concerns is "We have about 30 minutes for our visit today, and I want to ensure that I address your most important concerns. Tell me what you would like to discuss."

Key Concept: Physicians commonly need to triage patients’ concerns during visits. Physicians should prioritize patients’ concerns along with their most medically urgent concerns.

Explanation: Communicating about time limitations can be challenging. Physicians should set gentle boundaries with regard to what can be accomplished during an appointment while inviting the patient’s input on which concerns to prioritize.

Differential: The physician should avoid commenting on a patient’s abundance of concerns, which can be perceived as dismissive and may elicit shame or invalidate the patient’s feelings.

Incorrect Answers: A, B, C, and D.

Choice A: "Considering your medical history, I will not be able to address all of your issues in the next 30 minutes. I hope you are willing to come back again soon” is inappropriate. Rather than immediately focusing on what can’t be addressed, the physician should partner with the patient to set priorities for the visit. Additionally, the physician should avoid commenting on the patient’s abundance of issues, as this approach may imply that the patient is uniquely challenging and may come across as a judgment.

Choice B: "I'm concerned that you have too many issues to address at our visit today. On your next visit, I will ask the receptionist to schedule us more time” is inappropriate. The physician should avoid commenting on the amount of patient concerns, as this is a dismissive response that may elicit shame or invalidation.

Choice C: "I imagine that you have many issues to discuss today. Let me address your health issues first, and then you can tell me what you would like to talk about” is invalidating as it implies that the patient’s concerns are not legitimate health concerns.

Choice D: "I'd like to check in with you today about all of your medical issues. I suggest we start with your most serious medical condition” is incorrect. Though it does invite the patient’s collaboration, instead of inviting the patient to share their top concerns, this statement instructs the patient to interpret their most “serious” condition. The most “serious” condition may not align with the patient’s priorities.

questions.stemHtml: A 72-year-old woman with osteoporosis is brought to the emergency department because of a 1-hour history of severe chest pain. She also has a 1-month history of episodic chest pain and difficulty swallowing. She underwent open reduction and internal fixation for a right hip fracture 3 years ago, and she underwent a colectomy for colon cancer 2 years ago. Current medications are alendronate, calcitonin, and a multivitamin. She says that she takes all her medications just before going to bed at night. Her voice is hoarse. Her pulse is 110/min, respirations are 18/min, and blood pressure is 140/90 mm Hg. Physical examination shows no other abnormalities. Which of the following is the most likely cause of the chest pain in this patient?
questions.explanationHtml:
Correct Answer: B.

Educational Objective: Gastroesophageal reflux disease (GERD) typically presents with burning epigastric and lower chest pain, as seen in this patient, often in association with consumption of a large meal or trigger food. Acid reflux in the esophagus causes mucosal irritation and inflammation, which can present as mucosal erythema, hyperplasia, eosinophilic infiltrate, and erosions in reflux esophagitis. Alendronate can cause erosive esophagitis, especially if taken just before going to bed.

Evaluation: GERD presents with chest discomfort, often in association with consumption of a large meal or trigger food such as an acidic beverage, fatty foods, coffee, chocolate, or tomatoes. GERD is often worse with supine positioning.

Definition: Acid reflux in the esophagus causes mucosal irritation and inflammation, which can present as chest discomfort, mucosal erythema, hyperplasia, eosinophilic infiltrate, and erosions in reflux esophagitis. Over time, if GERD remains untreated, metaplasia can occur, leading to Barrett esophagus, a state of premalignancy marked by intestinal metaplasia of the distal esophagus. Barrett esophagus can subsequently lead to esophageal adenocarcinoma. Other complications of untreated GERD include esophageal strictures.

Prevention: Avoiding risk factors including trigger foods and medications (eg, NSAIDs and bisphosphonates), tobacco, and eating directly before bed decreases the risk for erosive esophagitis.

Treatment: Omeprazole irreversibly inhibits the H+/K+–ATPase in gastric parietal cells. Decrease in stomach acid production allows for neutralization of stomach contents, limiting the inflammatory and erosive sequelae of GERD in the distal esophagus, and allowing for appropriate healing of previous esophagitis. H2-receptor blocking agents may also be used.

Differential: Alendronate has been associated with chemical esophagitis. It is recommended that patients consume the medication with plenty of water and that they stay upright for at least 30 minutes after taking it. This patient’s routine of taking it right before bed, combined with her hoarse voice, chest pain, and difficulty swallowing, are most suggestive of erosive esophagitis.

Incorrect Answers: A, C, D, and E.

Choice A: Aortic dissection is incorrect. This life-threatening emergency classically presents as tearing chest or abdominal pain radiating to the back, often with a peripheral pulse or blood pressure deficit, and with neurologic symptoms such as numbness or tingling in an extremity. Chronic, episodic chest pain and a hoarse voice are not consistent with this diagnosis.

Choice C: Fat embolus is incorrect. Fat embolism typically occurs acutely after long bone or pelvic fractures due to fat macroglobule embolization to the pulmonary and systemic circulation. Presentation can include the classic triad of hypoxemia, petechial rash, and neurologic derangements. The patient has no risk factors for a fat embolism, and episodic chest pain with a hoarse voice is more consistent with erosive esophagitis.

Choice D: Rib fracture is incorrect. Rib fracture is a common cause of acute chest pain particularly in younger patients, who are more likely to sustain injuries from trauma (eg, motor vehicle collision, sports). Rib fractures are rarely spontaneous and are unlikely in a patient who lacks a history of trauma.

Choice E: Thoracic metastasis is incorrect. While the lung is a common area of metastasis for colon cancer, presentation is usually characterized by cough, dyspnea, and chronic chest discomfort. If there is metastasis to the ribs or thoracic spine, pain can be severe but is typically not episodic.

questions.stemHtml: A 65-year-old man comes to the office with his wife because of frequent fainting episodes during the past week. The episodes, which begin suddenly and last for about 10 seconds, usually occur when he is standing. There are no signs of seizure. He takes no medications. He has a sedentary lifestyle. Pulse is 43/min, respirations are 16/min, and blood pressure is 90/40 mm Hg. Physical examination shows no abnormalities. ECG is shown. Which of the following alterations in brain metabolism is the most likely cause of this patient's symptoms?

options.label: D
options.html: D. Lack of free fatty acids

questions.explanationHtml:
Correct Answer: F.

Educational Objective: This patient’s symptoms of frequent fainting episodes in the setting of bradycardia and hypotension are consistent with Adams-Stokes syncope. The frequent fainting episodes are caused by bradycardia leading to impaired cerebral perfusion and lack of oxygen.

Evaluation: Adams-Stokes syncope classically presents with episodic fainting that results from bradycardia causing cerebral hypoperfusion due to the sudden decrease in cardiac output.

Definition: Adams-Stokes syncope is a sudden, transient loss of consciousness caused by a brief episode of severe bradycardia or asystole, most commonly caused by high-grade atrioventricular block as in this patient’s case. The abrupt drop in cardiac output leads to cerebral hypoperfusion and therefore a lack of cerebral oxygenation, resulting in syncope that may be accompanied by pallor or brief seizure-like activity. The diagnosis is established by ECG evaluation showing a bradyarrhythmia during symptoms, which may be recorded by a 24-hour ambulatory ECG monitoring device. Syncope is a natural response to limited oxygenation of the brain, and once cerebral perfusion is restored, the patient will regain consciousness if restoration of cerebral blood flow and oxygenation occurs prior to irreversible neuronal ischemia.

Prevention: Prevention and treatment of Adams-Stokes syncope is through permanent pacemaker implantation, which is also used to treat the condition.

Treatment: The primary treatment for Adams-Stokes syncope and resultant lack of cerebral oxygenation because of bradyarrhythmia is the implantation of a permanent pacemaker.

Differential: Fainting episodes, which have many potential causes, are characterized by impaired central nervous system perfusion and oxygenation. In this specific case, the patient’s vital signs and ECG show bradycardia and hypotension, pointing to a cardiac cause of impaired cerebral perfusion.

Incorrect Answers: A, B, C, D, and E.

Choice A: Excess ammonia is incorrect. While excess ammonia is present in various diseases such as acute liver failure and urea cycle disorders and can present with encephalopathy, hyperammonemia would not present with fainting episodes. Hyperammonemia classically presents with impaired cognition accompanied by flapping hand tremor.

Choice B: Excess bicarbonate is incorrect. Excess bicarbonate is consistent with metabolic alkalosis or respiratory acidosis. While there can be many metabolic derangements associated with hypoperfusion, a lack of oxygenation, not an excess of bicarbonate, mediates syncope.

Choice C: Excess lactate is incorrect. Excess lactate can cause lactic acidosis and may result from hypoperfusion. While there can be many metabolic derangements associated with hypoperfusion, a lack of oxygenation, not an excess of lactate, mediates syncope.

Choice D: Lack of free fatty acids is incorrect. Fatty acid oxidation disorders may lead to a lack of free fatty acids and typically present with hypoketotic hypoglycemia. Lack of free fatty acids may cause light-headedness, seizure, arrhythmia, or impaired consciousness but would not present with severe bradycardia and intermittent fainting episodes with an ECG showing severe bradycardia.

Choice E: Lack of glucose is incorrect. Hypoglycemia can result in altered mental status and syncope; however, hypoglycemia would not also cause sinus bradycardia. Patients with hypoglycemia are often tachycardic due to activation of the sympathetic nervous system and may also present with seizure-like activity and tremors.

questions.stemHtml: A 66-year-old man is admitted to the intensive care unit for treatment of a myocardial infarction. An ECG shows ST-segment elevation in leads V2 through V4. Which of the following is the most likely finding on coronary artery catheterization?

options.label: A
options.html: A. Dissection of the proximal aortic root

options.label: B
options.html: B. Occlusion of the anterior interventricular (left anterior descending) artery

options.label: C
options.html: C. Occlusion of the atrioventricular artery

options.label: D
options.html: D. Occlusion of the coronary vein

options.label: E
options.html: E. Occlusion of the right coronary artery

questions.explanationHtml:
Correct Answer: B.

Educational Objective: ST-segment elevations in leads V2 through V4 localize to an anterior wall myocardial infarction, most commonly due to occlusion of the left anterior descending (LAD) artery. Recognizing ECG lead localization allows rapid identification of the affected coronary vessel in acute coronary syndromes.

Key Concept: Patients with anterior myocardial infarction present with chest pain and ECG findings of ST-segment elevation in leads V1 through V4 (most prominently in V2 through V4). Emergent coronary angiography typically shows occlusion of the LAD artery supplying the anterior wall of the left ventricle.

Explanation: The LAD artery branches from the left coronary artery and supplies the anterior wall of the left ventricle, anterior septum, and apex. Occlusion of this artery leads to anterior wall myocardial infarction, which is associated with high morbidity and mortality due to the large territory affected. On ECG, this corresponds to ST-segment elevations in the anterior precordial leads (V1 through V4). Risk factors include advanced age, hypertension, hyperlipidemia, smoking, and diabetes mellitus.

Differential: In this 66-year-old man with ST-segment elevations in leads V2 through V4, the infarction localizes to the anterior wall, which is supplied by the LAD artery. Other coronary artery occlusions produce distinct ECG patterns involving inferior or lateral leads.

Incorrect Answers: A, C, D, and E.

Choice A: Dissection of the proximal aortic root is incorrect. Aortic dissection classically presents with acute tearing chest pain radiating to the back or shoulder, along with paresthesias and neurologic impairments, or symptoms localizing ischemia to additional, noncardiac anatomic territories as the dissection limits perfusion to aortic branches. While aortic dissection can occlude coronary arteries, the right or left main coronary arteries would be affected, which would present with ST-segment elevation throughout the precordium, or in the inferior/posterior territory.

Choice C: Occlusion of the atrioventricular artery is incorrect. This typically refers to a branch of the right coronary artery supplying the atrioventricular node and is associated with inferior wall elevation or atrioventricular block, not anterior ST-segment elevations.

Choice D: Occlusion of the coronary vein is incorrect. Coronary veins drain deoxygenated blood from the heart (via the coronary sinus) and are not associated with arterial ischemia.

Choice E: Occlusion of the right coronary artery is incorrect. Right coronary artery occlusion typically causes inferior wall myocardial infarction with ST-segment elevations in leads II, III, and aVF, not V2 through V4.

questions.stemHtml: A 34-year-old man comes to the physician because of a 1-week history of temperatures to 39°C (102.2°F) and pain with urination. Physical examination shows generalized abdominal tenderness and right flank tenderness. Active extension of the right hip produces right flank pain. Urinalysis shows 100 WBC/hpf. Irritation of which of the following structures is the most likely cause of this patient's pain on hip extension?
questions.explanationHtml:
Correct Answer: E.

Educational Objective: This patient presenting with fever, dysuria, right flank pain, and pyuria most likely has pyelonephritis, a urinary tract infection that has spread to the kidneys. In cases of pyelonephritis, irritation of the nearby psoas muscle can lead to pain with hip extension.

Evaluation: Pyelonephritis may present with symptoms such as flank pain, fever, chills, nausea, vomiting, and costovertebral tenderness on physical examination. Pyelonephritis can cause irritation to structures adjacent to the kidneys including the psoas muscle, which is stretched during active hip extension.

Definition: Urinary tract infections, if untreated, may result in pyelonephritis due to the retrograde travel of bacteria up the ureters to the kidneys. Urinalysis typically is positive for leukocyte esterase and nitrites along with many WBCs and WBC casts on microscopy.

Prevention: Pyelonephritis may be prevented by the early identification and treatment of a urinary tract infection.

Treatment: Treatment of pyelonephritis includes prompt initiation of antibiotics. The most common bacteria resulting in the infection is Escherichia coli.

Differential: This patient presents with symptoms consistent with pyelonephritis, which can cause irritation to structures adjacent to the kidneys. The most likely cause of his flank pain on hip extension is irritation of the nearby psoas muscle as it is being stretched through this movement. The other structures are less likely to be associated with the patient’s pain, because unlike the psoas muscle, they are not stretched when the hip is extended, and irritation to them would cause pain in different regions (eg, thigh, groin, buttocks).

Incorrect Answers: A, B, C, D, and F.

Choice A: External iliac artery is incorrect. The external iliac artery does not lie in close proximity to the kidney as the aorta bifurcates inferiorly. Irritation of the psoas muscle is the more likely explanation.

Choice B: Femoral nerve is incorrect. Irritation of the femoral nerve may result in medial thigh and leg neuropathic pain. Irritation of the psoas muscle is more likely to produce flank pain.

Choice C: Genitofemoral nerve is incorrect. The genitofemoral nerve provides sensation to the medial thigh and groin. Irritation of the nerve would not likely produce flank pain.

Choice D: Piriformis muscle is not the most likely cause of this patient’s pain on hip extension. The piriformis muscle is located in the buttock and may be a cause of buttock pain. Pyelonephritis is unlikely to cause irritation of the piriformis.

Choice F: Testicular artery is incorrect. The testicular artery originates from the aorta near the level of the kidneys. Irritation of the psoas muscle is more likely in cases of pyelonephritis, which may result in flank pain on hip extension.

questions.stemHtml: A 38-year-old man comes to the physician's office because of impotence for the past 6 months. He also has a history of pain in his calves when walking, which subsides with rest. He has had type 1 diabetes mellitus for 24 years and has smoked ½ pack of cigarettes daily for the past 20 years. Erections occur in the morning when he awakens with a full bladder, but they are not firm enough to allow penetration during intercourse. His testicles are of normal size without masses, and his prostate is symmetric and slightly enlarged. Dorsalis pedis pulses are diminished bilaterally. Other pulses are normal. Examination of the lower extremities shows brawny discoloration of the skin consistent with venous stasis dermatitis. Which of the following is the most likely cause of his impotence?
questions.explanationHtml:
Correct Answer: A.

Educational Objective: The patient in this case is presenting with symptoms and risk factors for peripheral vascular disease. The most likely cause of this patient’s impotence is arterial insufficiency.

Evaluation: Peripheral vascular disease may present with symptoms of claudication, leg pain that occurs following exertion and improves with rest, decreased peripheral pulses, and erectile dysfunction.

Definition: Peripheral vascular disease is common among older male patients who have a significant smoking history and a history of hypertension, diabetes mellitus, or hyperlipidemia. The diagnosis is suggested by absent or diminished peripheral pulses, hairless legs with smooth skin that may ulcerate, and is further supported by a reduced ankle brachial index. CT scan, MRI, or conventional angiography can confirm the presence of arterial stenosis and atherosclerosis of the extremities.

Prevention: The risk for developing peripheral vascular disease can be decreased through the avoidance of smoking, eating a healthy diet, and with adequate blood pressure control.

Treatment: Engaging in a walking program is a first-line therapy along with mitigation of risk factors. Additional therapeutic options include cilostazol and surgical revascularization (eg, bypass, stenting).

Differential: The patient in this case with a history of long-standing type 1 diabetes mellitus as well as cigarette smoking has been found to have brawny discoloration of the lower extremities with venous stasis dermatitis and decreased dorsalis pedis pulses. These findings indicate a likely diagnosis of peripheral vascular disease. Arterial insufficiency in cases of peripheral vascular disease can lead to the development of erectile dysfunction.

Incorrect Answers: B, C, D, and E.

Choice B: Prostate inflammation is incorrect. Prostatitis may present with dysuria, frequency, and urinary urgency similar to a urinary tract infection. On examination, a tender, boggy, enlarged prostate can be palpated.

Choice C: Psychogenic sexual dysfunction is incorrect. Psychogenic sexual dysfunction may be considered if the patient has concerns regarding erectile dysfunction but continues to have erections while sleeping. In this case, the patient does have morning erections, but they are not firm enough to allow for penetration during intercourse, making another cause more likely.

Choice D: Testosterone deficiency is incorrect. Symptoms of testosterone deficiency include decreased endurance, fatigue, depression, decreased motivation, impaired memory, infertility, and decreased sex drive. The signs and symptoms in this case are more likely due to underlying peripheral vascular disease.

Choice E: Venous incompetence is incorrect. Venous incompetence may present with lower extremity edema, varicose veins, hyperpigmentation, and venous ulcerations. The patient in this case has been found to have decreased dorsalis pedis pulses with symptoms of claudication, which make arterial insufficiency more likely.

questions.stemHtml: A 76-year-old man with ankylosing spondylitis is brought to the emergency department 20 minutes after the sudden onset of severe lower thoracic pain and moderate upper abdominal pain. He has a 30-year history of essential hypertension. He was treated for bacterial endocarditis 5 years ago and syphilis 30 years ago. He has a family history of hemochromatosis. He has smoked 1½ packs of cigarettes daily for 50 years. His pulse is 104/min, and blood pressure is 160/100 mm Hg. A CT scan of the abdomen is shown. Which of the following is the greatest predisposing risk factor for this patient's current condition?
questions.explanationHtml:
Correct Answer: E.

Educational Objective: Cigarette smoking is the strongest modifiable risk factor for development of abdominal aortic aneurysm (AAA), which is this patient’s most likely condition. Chronic smoking promotes atherosclerosis and degradation of the aortic wall, leading to aneurysmal dilation.

Key Concept: AAA typically occurs in older men with risk factors such as long-term smoking and hypertension, often with abdominal, back, or flank pain when rapidly enlarging, ulcerating, rupturing, or dissecting. Diagnosis is confirmed with imaging such as abdominal CT scan or ultrasonography, which shows dilation of the abdominal aorta and may show complications such as penetrating ulceration, dissection, or rupture.

Explanation: An AAA is a localized dilation of the abdominal aorta, most commonly occurring below the renal arteries. The primary underlying mechanism involves degradation of connective tissue in the aortic wall due to chronic inflammation and atherosclerosis. Cigarette smoking is the most significant risk factor, increasing both formation and rupture risk. Additional risk factors include advanced age, male sex, and hypertension, all of which are present in this case.

Differential: In this older man who has smoked 1½ packs of cigarettes daily for 50 years and has a 30-year history of hypertension, smoking is the most significant contributor to AAA formation.

Incorrect Answers: A, B, C, and D.

Choice A: Ankylosing spondylitis is not the greatest predisposing factor for AAA in this patient. While associated with aortic pathology, ankylosing spondylitis is not generally associated with AAA as much as it is aortic root dilation or aortitis.

Choice B: Family history of hemochromatosis is incorrect. Hemochromatosis leads to iron overload affecting organs like the liver and heart but is not a major risk factor for AAA.

Choice C: History of bacterial endocarditis is incorrect. Endocarditis affects heart valves and may cause septic emboli but does not predispose to AAA.

Choice D: History of syphilis is incorrect. Tertiary syphilis can cause aortitis and aneurysms of the ascending thoracic aorta, but it generally does not affect the abdominal aorta as much as smoking.

questions.stemHtml: A 1-year-old boy is brought to the office for a follow-up examination. At birth, he was found to have tetralogy of Fallot, which was surgically corrected. He also has a seizure disorder treated with calcitriol, and he has had several severe upper respiratory tract infections since birth. Physical examination shows wide-set eyes, low ears with notched ear folds, and a small chin. Which of the following is the most likely mechanism of this patient's increased susceptibility to infections?

options.label: B
options.html: B. Failure of immunoglobulin class switching

options.label: C
options.html: C. Formation of circulating immune complexes

questions.explanationHtml:
Correct Answer: A.

Educational Objective: This patient most likely has DiGeorge (22q11.2 deletion) syndrome, which leads to increased susceptibility to infection as a result of defective T-cell immunity.

Key Concept: DiGeorge syndrome results from failure of development of the third and fourth pharyngeal pouches, leading to thymic aplasia and impaired T-cell maturation.

Explanation: This patient has classic features of DiGeorge syndrome, including a congenital heart defect (tetralogy of Fallot), hypocalcemia due to parathyroid aplasia (likely causing his seizure disorder and treated with calcitriol), recurrent infections, and characteristic facial anomalies. Aplasia or hypoplasia of the thymus leads to decreased T cells, resulting in impaired cell-mediated immunity and increased susceptibility to viral, fungal, and intracellular infections.

Differential: This patient’s constellation of cardiac defects, hypocalcemia, immunodeficiency, and facial anomalies narrows the differential to DiGeorge syndrome rather than another cause of immunocompromise.

Incorrect Answers: B, C, D, and E.

Choice B: Failure of immunoglobulin class switching is incorrect. Failure of immunoglobulin class switching causes immunodeficiency with increased IgM resulting in impaired acquired immunity.

Choice C: Formation of circulating immune complexes is incorrect. Circulating immune complex deposition is the pathophysiology of systemic lupus erythematosus, which presents with rash, fever, joint pain, pulmonary and renal inflammation, and cytopenias.

Choice D: Hyper IgE is incorrect. Hyper IgE syndrome presents with eczema in addition to immunocompromise, not congenital cardiac defects and hypocalcemia, as seen in this patient.

Choice E: Lack of superoxide production is incorrect. Chronic granulomatous disease is caused by a lack of superoxide production, resulting in immunodeficiency in which neutrophils cannot execute the respiratory burst to generate free radicals. Chronic granulomatous disease is not associated with cardiac defects or hypocalcemia.

questions.stemHtml: A 45-year-old man is admitted to the hospital because of a 4-month history of fatigue, constipation, nausea, and decreased concentration; he also has had a 5-kg (11-lb) weight loss during this period. He appears cachectic. Physical examination shows generalized, diffuse weakness. Serum studies show a calcium concentration of 14 mg/dL. He is diagnosed with metastatic renal cell carcinoma. In addition to intravenous 0.9% saline and a bisphosphonate, a diuretic that enhances renal calcium excretion is prescribed. The most likely mechanism of action of this medication occurs at which of the following labeled locations in the diagram of a nephron?
questions.explanationHtml:
Correct Answer: D.

Educational Objective: Loop diuretics act at the thick ascending limb of the loop of Henle, which corresponds to the location labeled D on the diagram shown, to decrease solute and fluid reabsorption. Loop diuretics increase calcium secretion and may be used in cases of hypercalcemia, as in this patient.

Key Concept: The ascending limb of the loop of Henle is the site of action of loop diuretics. Examples of loop diuretics include furosemide, torsemide, bumetanide, and ethacrynic acid.

Explanation: Loop diuretics act on the sodium-potassium-chloride cotransporter to decrease solute reabsorption. As a result of decreased solute reabsorption, less water is reabsorbed by osmotic pull. This leads to a total decrease in body fluid volume or volume contraction. In addition, loop diuretics may result in electrolyte changes such as hyponatremia, hypokalemia, hypochloremia, hypomagnesemia, and hypocalcemia.

Differential: This patient presents with symptomatic hypercalcemia, which is treated with loop diuretics. The ascending limb of the loop of Henle, labeled D on the diagram shown, is the site of action of loop diuretics. The other labeled locations represent the site of action for different classes of diuretics that would not be used in hypercalcemia, or in the case of labels B and C, are not significant sites of diuretic action.

Incorrect Answers: A, B, C, E, and F.

Choice A: The proximal convoluted tubule is incorrect. The proximal convoluted tubule is the site for reabsorption of the majority of electrolytes (bicarbonate, sodium, chloride, phosphate, and potassium), water, uric acid, glucose, and amino acids. questions.stemHtml: A 70-year-old man undergoes a colonoscopy for cancer screening. He has no symptoms. Colonoscopy shows numerous pouches as shown in the photograph. These anomalies are most likely located in which of the following portions of the sigmoid colon wall?

options.label: A
options.html: A. At the sites of mucosal folds

options.label: B
options.html: B. At the sites of penetration of vasa recta into the smooth muscle layer

options.label: C
options.html: C. At the sites of prior tubular adenomas

options.label: D
options.html: D. At the sites of recurrent tubular adenomas

options.label: E
options.html: E. At the sites of submucosal degeneration

questions.explanationHtml:
Correct Answer: B.

Educational Objective: The colonoscopy findings in this patient are suggestive of diverticulosis, which is characterized by sac-like protrusions of the colonic wall and is hypothesized to develop secondary to increased intraluminal pressure that predisposes the herniation of mucosa and submucosa through the muscularis propria. This occurs at the sites of penetration of vasa recta into the smooth muscle layer of the sigmoid colon wall.

Key Concept: Diverticula are outpouchings of the mucosal and submucosal layers into the muscular layer that occur at weak points in the gut wall where the small arterioles of the vasa recta penetrate the muscularis.

Explanation: The layers of the gastrointestinal wall, from the luminal surface to the exterior of the bowel, include the mucosa, submucosa, muscularis propria, and serosa. Diverticulosis is characterized by sac-like protrusions of the colonic wall and is hypothesized to develop secondary to increased intraluminal pressure that predisposes the herniation of mucosa and submucosa through the muscularis propria. This may happen most commonly in the sigmoid colon because the diameter of the sigmoid is smaller than other parts of the colon, so abnormal peristalsis in this area causes higher intraluminal pressure compared to other segments. Risk factors for the development of diverticulosis include abnormal colonic motility, high dietary intake of red meat and low dietary fiber, physical inactivity, and obesity. Complications of diverticular disease include bleeding and diverticulitis.

Differential: Colonic diverticula are categorized as false or pseudodiverticula because they involve herniation of the mucosa and submucosa through the muscularis rather than outpouching of all layers of the organ wall. Penetration of the vasa recta into the muscularis creates mechanical weak points that can fail and allow the formation of these structures.

Incorrect Answers: A, C, D, and E.

Choice A: At the sites of mucosal folds is incorrect. Called haustral folds in the colon, these dynamic structures are formed by contraction of the inner layer of the muscularis, which runs circumferentially. They are not sites of mechanical weakness. Effacement of the haustra can be seen in ulcerative colitis.

Choice C: At the sites of prior tubular adenomas is incorrect. While prior resection of a lesion could theoretically cause a weak point because of scar tissue, the scar tissue would be in the mucosal or submucosal layer (from which the lesions originate), not the muscularis, and would therefore be less likely to form a diverticulum.

Choice D: At the sites of recurrent tubular adenomas is incorrect. While some literature suggests that patients with diverticulosis are more likely to have adenomas on colonoscopy, this is thought to be because of their similar risk factors (eg, increasing age, low dietary fiber).

Choice E: At the sites of submucosal degeneration is incorrect. While age-related loss of elasticity of multiple layers of the colonic wall has been implicated in the pathogenesis of diverticulosis, the weak points caused by the penetration of vasa recta into the muscularis are more likely to result in the formation of diverticula.

questions.stemHtml: A previously healthy 36-year-old woman is brought to the emergency department 30 minutes after the onset of progressive shortness of breath and chest pain. There is no history of trauma. Her temperature is 37.1°C (98.8°F), respirations are 32/min and labored, and blood pressure is 136/72 mm Hg. Pulse oximetry on room air shows an oxygen saturation of 88%. Physical examination shows decreased breath sounds over the right side of the chest. A PA chest x-ray is shown. Which of the following is the most likely cause of this patient's condition?
questions.explanationHtml:
Correct Answer: E.

Educational Objective: Sudden onset dyspnea and pleuritic chest pain with unilateral absence of lung markings on chest x-ray as seen in this patient is characteristic of a pneumothorax. Decreased breath sounds on the affected side help distinguish pneumothorax from other causes of acute respiratory distress.

Evaluation: This previously healthy 36-year-old woman presents with acute shortness of breath, pleuritic chest pain, tachypnea, and hypoxemia, which are typical features of a spontaneous pneumothorax. The PA chest x-ray showing absent lung markings in the right lung field confirms the presence of air in the pleural space.

Definition: Pneumothorax occurs when air enters the pleural space, leading to partial or complete lung collapse and absence of normal respiratory mechanics due to loss of negative intrapleural pressure. Primary spontaneous pneumothorax can occur in otherwise healthy individuals, often as a result of rupture of subpleural blebs. Secondary pneumothorax occurs in patients with underlying lung disease or trauma. Accumulation of air prevents lung expansion, resulting in decreased breath sounds and hypoxemia. Large or rapidly expanding pneumothoraces can progress to a tension pneumothorax, resulting in hemodynamic compromise due to obstructive shock from impaired venous return.

Prevention: There are no specific preventive measures for primary spontaneous pneumothorax, although smoking cessation decreases risk. Patients with recurrent pneumothoraces may benefit from pleurodesis to prevent future incidence.

Treatment: Management depends on size and clinical stability and ranges from supplemental oxygen and observation in mild cases to needle aspiration or chest tube placement in moderate to severe cases. Emergent decompression is required if a tension pneumothorax is suspected.

Differential: The patient’s acute onset symptoms, unilateral decreased breath sounds, and absence of lung markings on PA chest x-ray are typical for pneumothorax. The absence of trauma and preserved blood pressure argue against other acute cardiopulmonary causes.

Incorrect Answers: A, B, C, and D.

Choice A: Cardiac tamponade is incorrect. Cardiac tamponade presents with hypotension, jugular venous distension, and muffled heart sounds, rather than unilateral absent breath sounds or loss of lung markings. Cardiac tamponade generally presents with a normal chest x-ray as well, as the fluid in the pericardial space is not radiographically distinct from myocardium and blood.

Choice B: Diaphragmatic hernia is incorrect. Diaphragmatic hernia typically causes bowel sounds in the chest, and the bowel would also be visible on x-ray. Diaphragmatic hernia may follow trauma in an adult or be congenital in a newborn; it would not present with sudden unilateral lung collapse in a healthy adult patient.

Choice C: Hydrothorax is incorrect. Hydrothorax refers to the accumulation of serous fluid in the pleural space and would cause opacification, not the absence of lung markings on chest x-ray. Hydrothorax is often associated with liver dysfunction/cirrhosis when present in isolation on the right side of the chest.

Choice D: Pleural effusion is incorrect. Pleural effusions produce blunting of the costophrenic angle and fluid levels on imaging rather than a radiolucent area without lung markings.

questions.stemHtml: A 38-year-old woman with Marfan syndrome is brought to the emergency department (ED) by her boyfriend because of a dislocated jaw. She was seen in the ED 8 weeks ago because of a rib fracture and sprained ankle. She says she is still unsteady on her ankle and dislocated her jaw when she rose from a stool and fell. She underwent aortic root repair with prosthetic aortic valve placement 7 years ago. Current medications are warfarin and acetaminophen. Vital signs are within normal limits. Physical examination shows diffuse facial edema; there is tenderness to palpation and poor dentition. Cardiac examination discloses a mechanical click. The patient is admitted to the hospital for heparin bridging before undergoing surgical repair of the jaw. Additional history regarding which of the following is most appropriate to obtain at this time?
questions.explanationHtml:
Correct Answer: D.

Educational Objective: Recurrent injuries with inconsistent or unlikely mechanisms should prompt evaluation for intimate partner violence (IPV), even in patients with underlying medical conditions (such as this patient with Marfan syndrome) that predispose to trauma. Identifying abuse is critical to prevent further harm and ensure patient safety, making it most appropriate in this case to obtain additional history regarding the patient’s relationship with her boyfriend.

Evaluation: IPV often presents with repeated emergency department visits for injuries at different stages of healing and explanations that do not fully account for or are inconsistent with injury severity. Evaluation requires a private, supportive history focused on the patient’s relationships and safety rather than relying solely on physical findings. Injuries should also be assessed and managed.

Definition: IPV is physical, emotional, financial, or sexual abuse inflicted by a current or former intimate partner. Risk factors include prior injury, social isolation, and dependence on a partner, but IPV can occur without such risk factors in any context. Victims may attribute injuries to accidents or underlying conditions, in effect masking abuse. Facial injuries, dental trauma, and recurrent fractures are common manifestations. Failure to recognize IPV can lead to escalating violence and morbidity or mortality.

Prevention: Routine screening for IPV in health care settings helps identify victims early and decrease future injury. Even basic questions such as “Do you feel safe at home and in your relationships?” can provoke affirmative responses from patients undergoing IPV. Providing resources, safety planning, and social support can interrupt ongoing abuse.

Treatment: Management focuses on ensuring immediate safety, validating the patient’s experience, and connecting the patient with social work, counseling, and protective resources. Medical treatment of injuries should be accompanied by appropriate reporting and support when indicated.

Differential: Although this patient has Marfan syndrome, which can predispose to musculoskeletal injuries, the pattern of repeated trauma, facial injury, poor dentition, and an implausible mechanism (sprained ankles heal in 2 to 4 weeks in general) raises concern for abuse. The presence of a boyfriend accompanying her to the emergency department makes it especially important to assess the nature of that relationship without the boyfriend present. Use of alcohol, contraceptives, illicit drugs, and tobacco would not explain the recurrent injury pattern and explanations inconsistent with injury severity.

Incorrect Answers: A, B, C, and E.

Choice A: Alcohol use is incorrect. Alcohol use can increase fall risk but does not explain the recurrent facial and skeletal injuries with inconsistent explanations.

Choice B: Contraceptive use is incorrect. Contraceptive use is not relevant in the context of recurrent injuries in this case.

Choice C: Illicit drug use is incorrect. Illicit drug use could increase this patient’s risk for falls, or increase the likelihood of her sustaining assault, but it is not as important to elicit this history as it is to assess for IPV. Her presentation is more suggestive of IPV with recurrent injuries without full explanation. Substance use may contribute to accidents but does not account for the concerning injury pattern and social context.

Choice E: Tobacco use is incorrect. Tobacco use increases her risk for cardiovascular disease, cancer, hypertension, stroke, and blood clots, which are unrelated to her recurrent injury pattern.

questions.stemHtml: A 53-year-old man comes to the office because of a 4-hour history of acute, severe pain in his left great toe that began during the middle of the night while he was sleeping. He rates the pain as a 10 on a 10-point scale and says that acetaminophen has not provided any relief. He works as a banker and reports that, earlier in the night, he went out to eat at a steak restaurant with clients. The patient has a history of hypertension and hyperlipidemia. Current medications are hydrochlorothiazide, atorvastatin, and daily aspirin. He is 165 cm (5 ft 5 in) tall and weighs 95 kg (210 lb); BMI is 35 kg/m2. Pulse is 93/min, respirations are 19/min, and blood pressure is 145/90 mm Hg. Physical examination shows inflammation of the left first metatarsophalangeal joint with early evidence of dactylitis. The most appropriate pharmacotherapy for this patient will include a drug that inhibits the activity of which of the following?
questions.explanationHtml:
Correct Answer: A.

Educational Objective: A middle-aged male presenting with acute, severe left great toe pain and inflammation with a history of red meat ingestion and hydrochlorothiazide use most likely has gout. The first-line treatment for acute gout is NSAIDs, which inhibit cyclooxygenase.

Key Concept: Acute gout is treated with NSAIDs, which inhibit cyclooxygenase.

Explanation: Gout is an acute monoarticular arthropathy resulting from an intra-articular inflammatory reaction to precipitation of monosodium urate crystals within the joint space. Gout can result from overproduction of uric acid, but more commonly occurs following the underexcretion of uric acid. Gout typically presents with acute, atraumatic single-joint pain, erythema, and swelling, which can recur in patients that are under- or untreated. The most common joint involved is the first metatarsophalangeal, but other common joints include the knees and elbows. Treatment consists of NSAIDs, colchicine, and/or corticosteroids for acute exacerbations. Chronic preventive management involves the use of xanthine oxidase inhibitors such as allopurinol. Additionally, patients should avoid triggering risk factors such as purine-rich meals and heavy alcohol consumption.

Differential: Acute gout is treated with NSAIDs, which inhibit cyclooxygenase. Interleukin-1 (IL-1) and tumor necrosis factor-α are increased in inflammatory states but not directly acted on by NSAIDs. Allopurinol, an inhibitor of xanthine oxidase, can be used to prevent future episodes of gout but is not used acutely.

Incorrect Answers: B, C, and D.

Choice B and Choice C: Interleukin-1 (IL-1) and tumor necrosis factor-α are incorrect. IL-1 and tumor necrosis factor-α may be increased in acute gout but are not directly acted on by NSAIDs. Conditions such as rheumatoid arthritis may present with joint pain and swelling; however, they usually do not affect solely the great toe.

Choice D: Xanthine oxidase is not the most appropriate pharmacotherapy. Allopurinol is used to decrease the serum urate concentration in patients with a history of multiple gout attacks to prevent additional episodes. Allopurinol is not used to treat acute gout.

He works as a banker and reports that, earlier in the night, he went out to eat at a steak restaurant with clients. The patient has a history of hypertension and hyperlipidemia. Current medications are hydrochlorothiazide, atorvastatin, and daily aspirin. He is 165 cm (5 ft 5 in) tall and weighs 95 kg (210 lb); BMI is 35 kg/m2. Pulse is 93/min, respirations are 19/min, and blood pressure is 145/90 mm Hg. Physical examination shows inflammation of the left first metatarsophalangeal joint with early evidence of dactylitis. The most appropriate pharmacotherapy for this patient will include a drug that inhibits the activity of which of the following?

questions.stemHtml: A 48-year-old woman undergoes lumpectomy of an infiltrating ductal carcinoma of the left breast. Histologic examination of the tumor specimen shows numerous mononuclear immune cells and associated areas of individual necrotic tumor cells. Which of the following mechanisms best describes this immune-mediated tumor cell damage?

options.label: A
options.html: A. FAS ligand expressed by tumor cell comes into contact with macrophages and this initiates apoptosis

options.label: B
options.html: B. Fc receptor on B lymphocytes binds to altered tumor cell membrane protein

options.label: C
options.html: C. Tumor cell protein induces macrophages to secrete cytokines that promote phagocytosis

options.label: D
options.html: D. Tumor cell protein is recognized by CD4+ T lymphocytes after entering class I MHC antigen-processing pathway

options.label: E
options.html: E. Tumor cell protein is recognized by CD8+ T lymphocytes after entering class I MHC antigen-processing pathway

questions.explanationHtml:
Correct Answer: E.

Educational Objective: Recognition of tumor antigens by CD8+ T lymphocytes via class I MHC is the principal immune mechanism responsible for targeted tumor cell death.

Key Concept: Tumor cell destruction by cytotoxic T lymphocytes occurs when tumor antigens are presented on class I MHC molecules and recognized by CD8+ T lymphocytes, leading to apoptosis of tumor cells.

Explanation: Endogenous tumor proteins are processed in the cytosol and presented on class I MHC molecules. Cytotoxic CD8+ T lymphocytes recognize these antigens via the T-lymphocyte receptor and induce apoptosis through perforin/granzyme release or FAS ligand interactions. This immune response produces targeted killing of individual tumor cells rather than widespread necrosis. Tumor-infiltrating lymphocytes are associated with improved prognosis in some cancers, reflecting effective immune surveillance.

Differential: This patient has infiltrating ductal carcinoma with numerous mononuclear immune cells and focal necrosis of individual tumor cells. This pattern is characteristic of cell-mediated immunity, specifically cytotoxic T lymphocyte–mediated tumor cell death.

Incorrect Answers: A, B, C, and D.

Choice A: FAS ligand expressed by tumor cell comes into contact with macrophages and this initiates apoptosis is incorrect. FAS ligand–mediated apoptosis is initiated by cytotoxic T lymphocytes, not by tumor cells engaging macrophages.

Choice B: Fc receptor on B lymphocytes binds to altered tumor cell membrane protein is incorrect. Antibody-dependent cellular cytotoxicity involves Fc receptors on NK cells or macrophages, not B lymphocytes.

Choice C: Tumor cell protein induces macrophages to secrete cytokines that promote phagocytosis is incorrect. Macrophage cytokine secretion may enhance inflammation but does not explain selective tumor cell apoptosis; further, tumor cells that are intact and located within a stromal matrix are targets of phagocytosis after lysis. Phagocytosis generally requires a cell to be free of stromal association, such as a motile bacterium, or a postapoptotic cell fragment.

Choice D: Tumor cell protein is recognized by CD4+ T lymphocytes after entering class I MHC antigen-processing pathway is incorrect. CD4+ T lymphocytes recognize antigens presented on class II MHC, not class I.

questions.stemHtml: A 65-year-old woman is evaluated in the intensive care unit 24 hours after admission from the emergency department, where imaging studies showed a large hemorrhagic stroke with brain stem herniation. She has been receiving ventilatory support since admission. A family meeting is attended by the patient's long-term partner, three siblings, and two children to discuss goals of care for the patient. After introducing the care team, which of the following is the most appropriate opening remark to the family?

options.label: A
options.html: A. “Do you know if your family member has completed an advance directive?”

options.label: B
options.html: B. “I appreciate you all being here, but ultimately decision-making will be up to the oldest child.”

options.label: C
options.html: C. “It is important that you designate a family spokesperson, so we know who to contact for all communications.”

options.label: D
options.html: D. “What do you know about what happened to your family member?”

questions.explanationHtml:
Correct Answer: D.

Educational Objective: Effective communication in critical care begins by assessing the family’s understanding of the patient’s condition. Open-ended questions such as “What do you know about what happened to your family member?” help establish shared understanding and guide compassionate, patient-centered discussions.

Key Concept: In family meetings for critically ill patients, clinicians should first determine what the family already knows about the situation. This approach helps identify misconceptions and tailor further discussion appropriately.

Explanation: Family-centered communication is a core component of critical care and end-of-life discussions. Starting with an open-ended question, such as asking what the family understands, allows the clinician to assess baseline knowledge and emotional readiness. This technique builds trust, avoids assumptions, and ensures that information is delivered at the appropriate level. It also facilitates shared decision-making by aligning medical information with the patient’s values and the family’s expectations. Given this patient’s hemorrhagic stroke and brain stem herniation, sensitive communication is especially important.

Differential: In this intensive care setting with a critically ill patient, the most appropriate first step is to assess the family’s understanding before discussing decisions or directives. This ensures that subsequent conversation is informed and compassionate.

Incorrect Answers: A, B, and C.

Choice A: “Do you know if your family member has completed an advance directive?” is not the most appropriate opening remark to the family. Although important, this question should come after establishing the family’s understanding of the situation and building rapport.

Choice B: “I appreciate you all being here, but ultimately decision-making will be up to the oldest child” is incorrect. Decision-making authority depends on legal designation first, and if no other decision-maker had been appointed, there is a specific order of decision-makers provided that all potential decision-makers know the patient, their values and preferences, and are of sound mind to make decisions themselves. Being the oldest child does not have any bearing on legal decision-making rights.

Choice C: “It is important that you designate a family spokesperson, so we know who to contact for all communications” is incorrect. While helpful for communication, this is not the appropriate opening step before assessing understanding.
